children.text: What confuses travellers in Egypt is less the danger and more the closeness.

People call out in markets. Around sites you'll hear "I can guide you." Cars, carriages, camels, souvenirs, photos, tips. Unlike countries where prices are posted silently and transactions end without conversation, the feel here is different.

Calling all of this "scam" makes Egypt look more frightening than it is. Going in unprepared, you can run into overcharging or unwanted guiding. What matters is not hostility — it is knowing how the system works.
In Egypt, decline clearly, set the price first, carry small notes, and don't accept guiding you didn't ask for. Those four alone make the trip considerably easier.
Bargaining is not rude
In Egyptian markets and around sites, bargaining is normal. At
Khan el-Khalili
, in souvenir shops, with camels and carriages, with individual taxis, and at craft shops, the first price is often not the final price.
Bargaining is not anger. It is conversation. The seller names a price; the buyer says what they want. If they meet, you buy; if not, you say thanks and move on.

In tourist-oriented markets, the first price can be high. You don't have to feel cheated every time. The seller wants a high price; you want a price you can be at peace with. Reading the gap between them is the market's etiquette.

The best move is not to buy at the first shop. Look at several shops, ask the price of similar pieces, see the quality differences, then bargain. Just walking the market once changes your sense of price.
Shopping at Khan el-Khalili
Khan el-Khalili in
Cairo

is a tourist-oriented market and a part of Islamic Cairo with a long commercial history. It grew up in the 1380s as a Mamluk commercial complex, and today mosques, shrines, workshops, spice shops, jewellery shops, and tourist shops layer together.

The atmosphere differs between the main tourist lanes and the slightly off-main streets where artisans and locals shop. The tourist lanes hold papyrus, lanterns, perfumed oils, scarves, copperware, alabaster, souvenirs — bargaining-based pricing. Side streets sometimes carry more practical shops and artisan workshops.

Before buying, confirm material. Real papyrus or banana-leaf substitute? Hand-hammered copper or machine-made? For silver, what is the weight and the stamp? For anything called antique, is it really exportable?

Genuine ancient antiquities are illegal to export. If told something is "a real piece of pharaonic Egypt," don't buy. What you should take home from Egypt is not archaeological artefact but modern craft and memories of the trip.
Watch out for informal guides
Common are unsolicited guides.
"This road is closed."
"The real market is this way."
"I'll take you to the government shop."
"There's a special festival today."
Not every approach is malicious. Many lead, in the end, to a specific shop, with a commission added into the price. Walking "freely," you can in fact be inside someone's commercial route.
If you want guiding, arrange a trusted guide in advance. Don't follow someone who approaches you at the entrance to a market or a site.
When declining, don't explain at length. Smile and say "No, thank you" or "La, shukran" and keep walking. Stopping to argue extends the conversation. Declining is not rude.
Common patterns around sites
At
Giza
, Saqqara, the
Luxor
west bank, and around
Aswan
, there are places with many approaches. Camels, carriages, photos, short guiding, souvenirs, tips. Setting conditions in advance is what matters here.
For camels or carriages, confirm the total before mounting. Per person or for the group? How many minutes? How far? Make it explicit so additional charges aren't demanded on dismount.

The same for photos. If someone takes your photo or appears with you in one, tips may be asked. If you don't want it, don't request it from the start. If you do, have a small tip ready. That alone reduces the unpleasant exchange.

Inside sites, if told "this isn't included in your ticket" or "I'll show you a special chamber," confirm with official staff or your guide. Tickets, separate fees, and photography rules vary by place. Don't pay in ambiguity.
Tipping and baksheesh
Egypt has a tipping culture. It is not only for tourists; it is broadly present as part of service.
Hotel porters, drivers, guides, boat crew, restaurants, restroom attendants, small help — situations where small tips are natural. Trying to refuse all of it makes the trip awkward.
You don't have to respond to every request. Unsolicited help, pushy approaches, meaningless guiding — you needn't pay.
What matters is carrying small notes. Only large bills makes tipping and shopping awkward. Keep Egyptian-pound small notes separate so you can produce them quickly; the exchanges go short.
Taxis and transfers
In Cairo and at tourist sites, confirming the price for transfers matters. For a non-metered taxi, set the price before riding. Destination, total, currency.
Where ride-hailing works, the price is visible — easier. At airports, hotels, and big sites, pickup points can be hard to find; allow time.
For long transfers and airport runs, don't pick on price alone. Car condition, driver trust, and time accuracy matter. For early-morning flights, late-night arrivals, Luxor–
Hurghada
moves, and desert transfers especially, use proper arrangements.
Currency and payment
At tourist sites, you'll sometimes hear prices in dollars or euros. Daily payments read better in Egyptian pounds. Paying in foreign currency leaves the other side's exchange rate ambiguous.
Before paying, confirm the notes. In an unfamiliar currency, denominations are easy to misread. Count change on the spot too. This is not distrust; it is normal verification.
Cards work at hotels and bigger shops; markets, small shops, tips, and short transfers want cash. ATMs are in major cities, but running short of cash on a site day is awkward. Prepare the day before.
How to decline
In Egypt, decline short, calm, and without repetition.
"No, thank you."
"La, shukran."
"Maybe later."
"I already have a guide."
That is enough. Trying hard to explain extends the conversation. If the other person keeps talking, keep walking. Don't get angry. Smiling and leaving is easier.

Even after being offered tea in a shop, you are not obliged to buy. If you sit long and have many items brought out, the seller will think a purchase is coming. If you don't intend to buy, thank them and leave early.
What you don't need to be afraid of
Being approached is not dangerous.
Bargaining is not dangerous.
Being asked for a tip is not unusual in Egypt.

What becomes a problem is moving in ambiguity. Riding without setting a price. Following unsolicited guiding. Paying without confirming currency. Wanting to decline but stopping to keep talking. Avoid those, and most friction shrinks.
Egyptian people are, in general, used to travellers. Many are kind. At tourist sites, commercial pressure is also there. Holding both at once is the most realistic posture.
To enjoy Khan el-Khalili

At Khan el-Khalili, don't make shopping the only point. Al-Hussein Square, al-Azhar surroundings, al-Muizz Street, the old mosques, cafés, the sound of the alleys. As part of Islamic Cairo, the market becomes much more interesting.

A famous spot like El Fishawy Café — a mint tea or coffee while watching the flow of people — has value on its own. Sit before you buy. Slow the market's pace a little. Negotiation gets more relaxed too.
For photos, ask or at least nod before pointing a camera at people. The market is not a tourist stage; it is where people work.

Near mosques and shrines, dress carefully. Don't expose shoulders or knees significantly. Respect prayer times and entry restrictions. Small considerations like these matter more than shopping technique.
Basics that make the trip easier
To reduce small troubles in Egypt, you don't need difficult skills.
Set the price in advance.
Carry small notes.
Don't accept unsolicited guiding.
Walk once before you buy.
Confirm currency and change.
Decline briefly.
Use trusted arrangements for important transfers.
That much is enough. You don't need to walk in suspicion. You also shouldn't leave everything to chance.
Egyptian markets and tourist areas are close, loud, and full of live transactions. To enjoy the energy, a little preparation helps. With it, the alleys of Khan el-Khalili,
the Giza plateau
, and the Luxor west bank all walk much more calmly.

deck: How to handle bargaining, tipping, bazaars, informal guides, and overcharging in Egypt — practical, without alarm.
